title: The Battle of Tours
objective_facts:
EXTRACTED VICTORY AND DEFEAT CONDITIONS
(taken directly from the trigger graph; score `objective` from
these, not from the objectives text)

Victory:
  - DESTROY_OBJECT on SALADIN (player 2) [path "[VC] Abd al-Rahman Slain"]
  - OBJECTS_IN_AREA on count 3, player 3, area (40,92)-(80,115) [path "[VC] Umayyad Withdrawal"]
Defeat:
  - DESTROY_OBJECT on WILLIAM_THE_CONQUEROR (player 1) [path "[Loss] Charles Martel Killed"]
  - OBJECTS_IN_AREA on count 10, player 2, area (40,15)-(80,35) [path "[Loss] Shield Wall Overrun"]
issues_found: Charles Martel is represented by the WILLIAM_THE_CONQUEROR hero unit — a named figure from 1066, over three centuries later. The engine ships no Martel hero, so a renamed generic Champion or Teutonic-style infantry hero should have stood in instead of another named Norman.
Abd al-Rahman al-Ghafiqi is represented by the SALADIN hero — a named Ayyubid sultan of 1187, and of a wholly different dynasty and region from the Umayyad emir of al-Andalus.
Duke Odo of Aquitaine is represented by EL_CID, a named Castilian of the 1090s; the Aquitanian ally is thus another wrong named historical person rather than a renamed generic.
Both active players are set to RANDOM civilization, so Frankish and Umayyad/Saracen architecture and unit bonuses are left to chance; nothing guarantees the period-appropriate look for either side.
Player 3 (the Aquitanians) appears to have no civilization assignment at all in the roster listing.

Umayyad force includes 6 KNIGHTs — heavy stirrup-and-lance cavalry — alongside camel riders and cavalry archers; the Berber and Arab horse at Tours were lighter, and the engine's Light Cavalry/Camel/Cavalry Archer mix alone would have been closer.
10 GOLD_MINEs and 8 STONE_MINEs are scattered on a one-day battlefield scenario with no economy, pure map-generation residue.
Force scale is tiny (about 20 Franks, 21 Umayyads) for an engagement the sources describe as involving armies of many thousands, though this is partly an engine convention.
strengths: Frankish roster is correctly infantry-only — MILITIA, MAN_AT_ARMS, SPEARMAN, PIKEMAN, CHAMPION — matching the sources' description of a dismounted Frankish phalanx with no cavalry of its own.
Umayyad roster is entirely mounted (camel riders, cavalry archers, knights) with a single villager, correctly casting the invaders as a cavalry army.
4,640 oak trees create the wooded high ground between Tours and Poitiers that the brief and the chronicles both emphasise as the Frankish advantage.

The trigger sequence reproduces the historical shape: successive cavalry charges against a holding line, an Aquitanian raid on the Umayyad baggage camp, Abd al-Rahman's death in the melee, and a nocturnal Umayyad withdrawal southward.

Victory conditions encode exactly the historical outcomes — slaying the enemy emir, or the enemy army physically withdrawing off the field to the south — and defeat on the leader's death or the line being overrun.
The 'like a wall, immovable as a block of ice' line is a genuine quotation from the Mozarabic Chronicle of 754.
October 732 dating and the Tours-Poitiers location are stated correctly.
justification: The scenario's structure, terrain, and objectives are strong: an infantry-only Frankish force holds a densely wooded ridge against an all-cavalry Umayyad army, with the Aquitanian camp raid, the emir's death, and the night withdrawal all encoded as real triggers, and victory/defeat turning on precisely the events the sources identify. The fatal flaw is the cast: all three commanders are represented by named heroes from the wrong centuries — William the Conqueror as Charles Martel, Saladin as Abd al-Rahman, and El Cid as Duke Odo — an entirely avoidable error, since renamed generic units were available. Leaving both civilizations RANDOM further abandons control over architecture and unit character for a scenario whose whole point is the contrast between Frankish foot and Arab-Berber horse.

title: Marco Polo on the Silk Road
objective_facts:
EXTRACTED VICTORY AND DEFEAT CONDITIONS
(taken directly from the trigger graph; score `objective` from
these, not from the objectives text)

Victory:
  - BRING_OBJECT_TO_AREA + OBJECTS_IN_AREA on WILLIAM_THE_CONQUEROR reaching area (100,52)-(116,68); count 1, player 1, area (0,0)-(119,119) [path "VC Victory"]
Defeat:
  - DESTROY_OBJECT on WILLIAM_THE_CONQUEROR (player 1) [path "Defeat Marco Dead"]
  - OBJECTS_IN_AREA on count 1, player 1, area (0,0)-(119,119) [path "Defeat Caravan Lost"]
issues_found: Marco Polo is represented by the WILLIAM_THE_CONQUEROR hero unit — a named eleventh-century Norman standing in for a thirteenth-century Venetian; the victory and defeat triggers key off him by that name, so the substitution is structural, not cosmetic. Renaming a generic unit was available.
Niccolo Polo is represented by the EL_CID hero — an eleventh-century Castilian, again a named figure from the wrong century and culture.

GENGHIS_KHAN is placed at the destination as the Khan the caravan is travelling to meet, but the Polos were received by Kublai Khan; Genghis died in 1227, 44 years before the journey's start. The engine ships no Kublai hero, so a renamed generic (or the Khan of the Mongol civ) was the correct fallback.
Both active players are left as civilization RANDOM, so architecture set, unit roster and language are unassigned — Shangdu may be rendered in Teutonic or Frankish stonework at random.

Shangdu is built from a CASTLE and two KEEPs, European fortification models rather than anything suggesting the Khan's summer palace; a walled compound of Mongol/Chinese-flavoured buildings was possible.

The escort is CROSSBOWMAN and KNIGHT — Western European heavy cavalry and crossbows for a merchant caravan that in fact travelled with local guides, camels and Mongol-issued safe-conduct; camels or trade carts existed in the catalogue.
Pack animals are modelled as SHEEP, which are herdable food rather than laden beasts; trade carts or camels would have carried the 'caravan goods' idea the defeat text asserts.
strengths: The route is staged as a genuine journey with correct sequential waypoints — Persian oasis, the Pamir 'Roof of the World', then Shangdu — matching the itinerary in the Travels.
Yurts (A-D), tents and a pavilion for the steppe raiders' camp, plus palm forest, cliffs and rock formations, give a plausible desert-and-mountain corridor.
The bandit player is composed of CAVALRY_ARCHER, LIGHT_CAVALRY and SCOUT_CAVALRY, an appropriate steppe raider profile, and is triggered as ambushes via PATROL rather than a standing army.
Dates and biography in the narration are correct: departure 1271, Niccolo's prior journey, Marco aged seventeen, roughly three years on the road, seventeen years in the Khan's service.

Victory is gated on delivering the Marco unit into the Shangdu area with at least one pack animal surviving, and defeat on his death or the loss of the animals — exactly the escort problem the history posed, with no elimination-of-enemy fallback.
justification: The trigger architecture and route staging are strong: victory is bringing Marco into the Shangdu box with a surviving pack animal, defeat is his death or the loss of the caravan, which is precisely the historical stake, and the Persia-Pamir-Shangdu waypoint sequence with steppe cavalry ambushes reproduces the shape of the journey. But the cast is badly wrong in avoidable ways — Marco is William the Conqueror, Niccolo is El Cid, and the Khan awaiting them at Shangdu is Genghis, dead 44 years before the Polos set out, where a renamed generic was the obvious remedy. Both civilizations are left RANDOM and Shangdu is a European Castle and Keeps, so the destination's architecture is unassigned and Latin rather than Mongol. Play would teach the correct itinerary and dates while showing the player three misnamed heroes at the key moments.

title: The Battle of Hastings
objective_facts:
EXTRACTED VICTORY AND DEFEAT CONDITIONS
(taken directly from the trigger graph; score `objective` from
these, not from the objectives text)

Victory:
  - DESTROY_OBJECT on KING (player 2) [path "[VC] Victory - Harold Slain"]
Defeat:
  - DESTROY_OBJECT on WILLIAM_THE_CONQUEROR (player 1) [path "[Defeat] William Slain"]
  - TIMER + OBJECTS_IN_AREA on 1800s elapsed; count 1, player 2, area (0,0)-(119,119) [path "[Defeat] Nightfall"]
issues_found: Both players are set to RANDOM civilization, so Norman/Anglo-Saxon architecture and unit bonuses are unassigned — a Frankish (Norman) vs Briton/Celt (Saxon) pairing was available and avoidable

2,560 oak trees on a 120x120 map turns Senlac into dense forest; the historical field was open downland with a ridge and marshy ground, and heavy woods contradict the cavalry manoeuvre and feigned-retreat tactics the brief centres on
Both armies are given permanent economic/production bases (TOWN_CENTER, BARRACKS, STABLE, ARCHERY_RANGE, BLACKSMITH, MONASTERY) for a single-day set-piece battle where neither side built anything
The 'Norman Reinforcements' trigger invents fresh riders arriving from the coast; William received no reinforcements at Hastings — his whole force was committed from the start
Force ratio is inverted: 30 Norman units (only 10 knights) against 51 Saxons, whereas the armies were roughly equal in size and the Norman advantage lay in its large mounted and archer contingents
Harold is represented by an unrenamed generic KING unit; since the engine ships no Harold hero this is an acceptable stand-in, but leaving it unnamed weakens identification
No archer arm for the Saxons is correct, but the Saxon SKIRMISHER count (10) reads as missile troops the shield wall largely lacked
strengths: WILLIAM_THE_CONQUEROR, the correct engine hero for the Norman commander, leads Player 1 and his death is the defeat condition — matching the real fragility of the invasion around William's person
Saxon core built from CHAMPION (axe-armed housecarls) plus massed SPEARMAN represents the shield wall well within the engine's vocabulary
Norman roster of KNIGHT + ARCHER + SPEARMAN correctly reflects the combined cavalry-archer-infantry assault
The feigned-retreat sequence is actually scripted: a hint trigger, a Saxon PATROL pursuit downhill, then an ambush that kills the isolated pursuers
Victory requires slaying Harold, and defeat occurs if Harold still lives at the 1800-second nightfall mark — exactly the historical win/lose condition for both sides
Narration dates the battle correctly to 14 October 1066 and names Senlac Hill, Harold Godwinson, and the housecarls
justification: The scenario gets the actors and the stakes right: the engine's own William hero leads a knight-archer-spearman force against a champion-and-spearman shield wall under a King standing in for Harold, and the encoded conditions — kill Harold before the 1800-second nightfall, lose if William falls — reproduce precisely the asymmetry of 14 October 1066. The scripted feigned retreat, Saxon PATROL pursuit, and ambush kill capture the battle's actual turning point. Setting is the weak point: both civilizations are left RANDOM despite Frankish and Briton being obvious choices, and 2,560 oaks bury the open Senlac ridge in forest while both sides are given Town Centres, stables, and blacksmiths for a one-day field engagement. The invented 'fresh Norman riders from the coast' reinforcement is the only outright fabrication in an otherwise faithful event sequence.

title: The Exile of El Cid
objective_facts:
EXTRACTED VICTORY AND DEFEAT CONDITIONS
(taken directly from the trigger graph; score `objective` from
these, not from the objectives text)

Victory:
  - DESTROY_OBJECT on SALADIN (player 2) [path "VC - Valencia Conquered"]
Defeat:
  - DESTROY_OBJECT on EL_CID (player 1) [path "Defeat - El Cid Falls"]
issues_found: Player 2's leader is the SALADIN hero — Saladin was a late-12th-century Ayyubid sultan in Egypt/Syria, a century after El Cid's death and 3,000 km away. The engine offers renamable generic units (and other Middle Eastern/Iberian heroes) that could have stood in for al-Qadir/Ibn Jahhaf of Valencia or the raider chief; using a famous hero from the wrong century and region is avoidable error.

Both active players are set to RANDOM civilization, so the architecture, unit roster and language of El Cid's Castilians and the Andalusi defenders are undefined at runtime — Spanish and Saracens were both available and obvious.

A single enemy player represents both Al-Mu'tamin's northern rivals (Aragon / al-Hayib of Lérida, who were Christian-allied Zaragozan enemies) and the city of Valencia, so the north-eastern 'raider camp' fields camel riders and cavalry archers under Saladin rather than anything resembling Aragonese or Lleidan troops.

Al-Mu'tamin of Zaragoza, El Cid's actual employer for most of the exile, exists only as dialogue text — no allied player, units or city, so the mercenary-service relationship that defines the period is never represented on the map.

The Almoravid intervention (Sagrajas 1086, Cuarte 1094) — the decisive military context of El Cid's Valencian years — is entirely absent, and the 1093-94 blockade/starvation of Valencia is reduced to a wall-breach assault.
El Cid's retinue is 4 knights with a Town Center and full building set, implying a settled lordship rather than the landless exile band described in the narration.
strengths: The EL_CID hero unit is correctly used for the protagonist, and his death as an instant defeat condition matches the brief's stated stake.
Chronology in the narration is accurate: banishment by Alfonso VI in 1081, service to Al-Mu'tamin of Zaragoza against his rivals, and the conquest of Valencia in 1094.
The reinforcement trigger after the first victory ('warriors flock to his banner') models the historical growth of El Cid's retinue through mercenary success.
Palm forest, coastal march 'south along the coast', and a heavily walled Valencia with castle and gate are plausible for the Mediterranean Levante.
Camel riders and cavalry archers are a reasonable engine abstraction for Andalusi/North African cavalry, given the catalogue.
justification: The scenario gets the narrative arc of El Cid's exile right in text — 1081 banishment, service to Al-Mu'tamin of Zaragoza, Valencia in 1094 — and correctly uses the EL_CID hero with his death as defeat. But the opposing force is led by the SALADIN hero, a figure a century later and a continent away, and victory is literally gated on killing Saladin, so the player 'conquers Valencia' by slaying an Ayyubid sultan; a renamed generic unit for al-Qadir or Ibn Jahhaf was available. Both civilizations are left RANDOM, so Castilian and Andalusi architecture and rosters are undefined, and Al-Mu'tamin — El Cid's actual patron — appears only as dialogue with no allied city or troops. The Almoravid wars that dominated the Valencian campaign are omitted entirely.

title: The Fall of Constantinople
objective_facts:
EXTRACTED VICTORY AND DEFEAT CONDITIONS
(taken directly from the trigger graph; score `objective` from
these, not from the objectives text)

Victory:
  - TIMER + DESTROY_OBJECT on 600s elapsed; MONASTERY (player 1) [path "[Victory] The Walls Hold"]
Defeat:
  - OBJECTS_IN_AREA on count 2, player 2, area (95,55)-(105,65) [path "[Defeat] Hagia Sophia Overrun"]
  - DESTROY_OBJECT on KING (player 1) [path "[Defeat] The Emperor Falls"]
  - DESTROY_OBJECT on MONASTERY (player 1) [path "[Defeat] The City Falls"]
issues_found: Player TWO's commander is the SALADIN hero unit — a 12th-century Ayyubid sultan standing in for Mehmed II, who died 260 years before 1453. The engine ships no Mehmed hero, so a renamed generic (e.g. a Cavalry Archer or Elite Janissary-equivalent) was the correct choice; placing a different named historical figure is avoidable error.

Both players are set to civilization RANDOM, so Byzantine and Turkish architecture, tech trees and unit bonuses are not guaranteed — the engine offers exactly Byzantines and Turks for this battle, making this a purely avoidable omission.

Ottoman roster includes CAMEL_RIDER x3, an Arab/Saracen unit inappropriate for the Rumelian and Anatolian troops at Constantinople, while the engine's Janissary (referenced in the text: 'Janissary regulars pour through the breach') is nowhere placed.
TREE_PALM_FOREST x10 is the vegetation placed for Thrace/the Bosphorus — palms are wrong for the Marmara littoral in April.

No water tiles, ships, or sea walls are present despite the brief and the objectives promising defence of the Golden Horn sea walls; the naval dimension (the chain, the Ottoman fleet portage, the Genoese relief squadron) is entirely absent.

Ottoman force is absurdly small (roughly 22 starting units plus a handful of waves) against a besieging army the sources put at 50,000–80,000; the asymmetry that defined the siege is inverted, with the defenders' 23 units nearly matching the attackers.
Only 3 bombard cannon and 2 mangonels represent Mehmed's siege train of some 60–70 guns including the Orban supergun; the 'great bombard roars' text is not matched by any distinguished large gun.
The Theodosian Walls are a single 57-tile stone wall line with no representation of the double wall, outer wall and moat that made the fortification famous.
strengths: Constantine XI is represented by a KING unit whose death triggers immediate defeat, correctly encoding the emperor's fall as the loss of the city.

A MONASTERY stands for the Hagia Sophia and is both a defeat condition (destroyed / overrun by 2 enemy units in the 95-105/55-65 area) and the thing that must survive to win — the right place is the stake.

The wave structure follows the historical sequence: probing attacks, sustained cannon bombardment, a scripted KILL_OBJECT wall breach with follow-up assault through the gap, weeks-of-siege interlude, then Mehmed's general assault of 29 May.
Giovanni Giustiniani's Genoese contingent arriving as reinforcement via CREATE_OBJECT is a genuine and well-chosen historical detail.
BOMBARD_CANNON is used for the Ottoman artillery, the correct engine analogue for the great guns that broke the walls.
Defender roster of archers, crossbowmen, spearmen and a few knights behind walls and keeps is a fair abstraction of the roughly 7,000 Greek and Italian defenders.
justification: The scenario gets the shape of the siege right — bombardment, a scripted breach, escalating assaults, Giustiniani's Genoese relief, and a victory keyed to outlasting the final assault while the Hagia Sophia monastery and the emperor-King survive, which is exactly the goal the defenders of 1453 actually had. It is undermined by the choice of SALADIN as the Ottoman commander, a named figure from the wrong dynasty and the wrong century when a renamed generic would have served, and by leaving both civilizations RANDOM when the engine ships Byzantines and Turks. The setting is further weakened by palm forest, a single-thickness wall line in place of the double Theodosian defences, and the complete absence of water or ships despite the objectives explicitly promising a defence of the Golden Horn sea walls.

title: The Rise of Temujin
objective_facts:
EXTRACTED VICTORY AND DEFEAT CONDITIONS
(taken directly from the trigger graph; score `objective` from
these, not from the objectives text)

Victory:
  - DESTROY_OBJECT on KING (player 2) [path "VC"]
Defeat:
  - DESTROY_OBJECT on GENGHIS_KHAN (player 1) [path "Defeat"]
issues_found: Both players are set to RANDOM civilization, so the Mongols are never actually assigned; the player's roster of CAVALRY_ARCHER and LIGHT_CAVALRY may be delivered by a Frankish or Teutonic tech tree with European architecture, undoing the steppe flavour the yurts establish.

Three distinct historical opponents — the Merkits, Jamukha's Jadaran, and the Naiman confederation — are all collapsed into a single Player 2 whose assets simply change ownership, so the player never faces them as separate powers and the shifting alliance structure of the steppe is invisible.

Jamukha, the blood-brother whose betrayal is the emotional centre of the brief, has no representative object at all: only a generic KING (Tayang Khan) and a VILLAGER_FEMALE (Borte) stand in for named figures. There is no evidence the KING was renamed, and a European crowned monarch is an odd stand-in for a Naiman khan when the engine offers cavalry-hero graphics.
Toghrul/Wang Khan of the Kereit, without whose army the rescue of Borte and much of Temujin's early rise is unintelligible, is entirely absent from both roster and narration.
Player 2 is given GUARD_TOWER x2 — permanent stone fortification is out of character for a nomadic Naiman camp, and avoidable given yurts and palisade options exist.

Narration places the alliance with Jamukha after Borte's rescue ('Her rescue binds the tribes closer... Jamukha rides to his side'), whereas the sources have Jamukha and Toghrul allied with Temujin for the Merkit campaign itself.
Jamukha's actual fate (defeat, capture and execution) is never resolved; his 'attack' is a single PATROL trigger with no objective attached.
strengths: GENGHIS_KHAN is the correct hero object for Temujin — the same man, not a figure from the wrong century — and the defeat condition on his death correctly encodes the fragility of the whole enterprise.
Victory is gated on the death of the Naiman KING standing in for Tayang Khan, i.e. the specific decisive decapitation of 1204 rather than a blanket wipe of all enemy units.
YURT_A through YURT_D used for both camps, plus sheep, deer, forage bushes and rock formations, give a recognisably pastoral-nomadic steppe settlement rather than castles and farms.
Force composition is horse-archer and light-cavalry heavy with only four villagers, appropriate to a small mobile warband rather than a settled economy.

The event sequence and dates are correct and in order: 1186 opening, Borte's abduction by the Merkits and rescue, alliance then rupture with Jamukha, destruction of the Naiman, kurultai of 1206 and the title 'Ruler of All Peoples'.
justification: The narrative spine is right — Borte's rescue, the Jamukha alliance and betrayal, the Naiman war, the 1206 kurultai — and the win/lose conditions correctly turn on killing the Naiman khan and on Temujin's own survival, which is what the history posed. The build undercuts this in two avoidable ways: both civilizations are left RANDOM despite the engine offering Mongols, and all three enemies (Merkit, Jadaran, Naiman) are one Player 2 whose units merely change hands, so Jamukha has no object at all and Tayang Khan is an unrenamed European KING. Toghrul of the Kereit, indispensable to the rescue of Borte, is missing entirely, and stone GUARD_TOWERs are a poor fit for a nomadic camp.

title: The Road to Reims
objective_facts:
EXTRACTED VICTORY AND DEFEAT CONDITIONS
(taken directly from the trigger graph; score `objective` from
these, not from the objectives text)

Victory:
  - DESTROY_OBJECT + DESTROY_OBJECT + BRING_OBJECT_TO_AREA on CHAMPION (player 2); CAVALIER (player 2); KING reaching area (104,56)-(112,64) [path "VC"]
Defeat:
  - DESTROY_OBJECT on KING (player 1) [path "Defeat"]
issues_found: Both players are set to RANDOM civilization, so the French escort column and the Anglo-Burgundian garrisons may appear with entirely wrong architecture and unit sets (e.g. Meso-American or East Asian buildings for Champagne towns) — the engine offers Britons and Franks/French, so this is avoidable.

The garrison commanders at Troyes and Chalons are unnamed generic units (a CHAMPION and a CAVALIER); no attempt is made to represent or rename any historical figure, and no French captains (La Hire, Duke d'Alencon, Poton de Xaintrailles — all available as renamed generics) accompany Joan, though they led the march.

Troyes and Chalons were held largely by Anglo-Burgundian garrisons, and both yielded by negotiation — Chalons opened its gates without a fight and Troyes capitulated once assault was prepared. The scenario's only encoded path is killing the enemy commander, so the brief's promise that garrisons 'can be fought or persuaded to surrender' is not implemented at all.

Terrain furnishing is generic random-map economy: 640 oak trees, 5 gold mines, 4 stone mines, 8 forage bushes and grazing sheep, with no roadway, river (the Seine/Marne), or town fabric linking Auxerre-Troyes-Chalons-Reims; the route the mission is about is not legible on the map.
Reims cathedral is represented only by a single GAIA MONASTERY with no surrounding city, which understates the coronation site that is the scenario's whole point.
Narration calls Charles 'the boy-king' — he was 26 in 1429; the boy-king of the period was Henry VI of England.
Auxerre, which also had to be passed and negotiated with on this march, is absent.
strengths: Joan of Arc is placed using the engine's actual Joan of Arc hero, the correct named figure for June-July 1429.
The Dauphin is represented by a KING unit, an apt engine stand-in whose survival and arrival drive the mission.

Victory is gated on the KING reaching a fixed cathedral area rather than on wiping out the enemy, matching the historical aim of the coronation march; defeat on the King's death mirrors the campaign's single indispensable asset.
The waypoint sequence Troyes -> Chalons -> Reims is in correct geographic and chronological order, with BRING_OBJECT_TO_AREA dialogue triggers marking each approach.
Text correctly situates the march after the deliverance of Orleans in June 1429 and ends with the anointing of Charles VII at Reims.
justification: The scenario gets the frame right — the real Joan of Arc hero, a KING standing in for the Dauphin, the Troyes-Chalons-Reims waypoints in order, and a victory condition that turns on escorting that King into the cathedral precinct rather than on annihilation. It is undermined by leaving both players' civilizations RANDOM, so the architecture and troop types of Champagne 1429 are left to chance, and by furnishing the route with random-map gold mines, stone mines and 640 oaks instead of towns and roads. Historically, Chalons opened its gates and Troyes capitulated after negotiation, yet the triggers permit only the killing of two anonymous generic commanders (a CHAMPION and a CAVALIER), so the brief's 'fought or persuaded to surrender' option is never built, and no French captain besides Joan is present. The narration is broadly truthful but calls the 26-year-old Charles a 'boy-king,' a description belonging to Henry VI.

title: The Siege of Vienna
objective_facts:
EXTRACTED VICTORY AND DEFEAT CONDITIONS
(taken directly from the trigger graph; score `objective` from
these, not from the objectives text)

Victory:
  - TIMER + OBJECTS_IN_AREA on 250s elapsed; count 1, player 1, area (42,69)-(48,75) [path "VC - Vienna Holds"]
Defeat:
  - DESTROY_OBJECT on TOWN_CENTER (player 1) [path "Defeat - Vienna Falls"]
  - DESTROY_OBJECT on KING (player 1) [path "Defeat - Commander Lost"]
issues_found: Both players are set to RANDOM civilization, so the defenders may appear with Aztec, Japanese or Mongol architecture and unit skins instead of a Central European (Teutons/Hungarians/Bohemians) garrison and an Eastern (Turks) besieger — an avoidable assignment error given the engine ships a Turks civ explicitly modelled on the Ottomans.
The brief's 'Spanish arquebusiers' are represented by 6 CROSSBOWMAN; the engine ships HAND_CANNONEER, the obvious gunpowder-infantry stand-in for 1529 arquebusiers, so the choice is avoidable.

The Ottoman roster contains no gunpowder infantry at all: janissaries, the core of Suleiman's assault troops at the Carinthian Gate, are absent (again HAND_CANNONEER or ELITE_JANISSARY were available), and the attackers are instead 5 CAMEL_RIDER, 4 LIGHT_CAVALRY and 6 CAVALRY_ARCHER — a steppe/desert cavalry force that did not storm Vienna's breaches.

Ottoman siege train includes BOMBARD_CANNON, MANGONEL and ONAGER; Suleiman's heavy artillery was in fact bogged down and left behind on the Danube march, which is why the siege turned on mining rather than battering — the placed content contradicts the scenario's own mine-centred narrative.
3,541 TREE_OAK dominate the map, making the Vienna plain and its trench/siege lines into dense forest; the historical approaches and Ottoman camp were open ground.
Both commanders are the same generic KING object, so Salm and Suleiman are visually indistinguishable and neither is characterised beyond dialogue.
No sapper/mine visual apparatus beyond a scripted KILL_OBJECT on a wall segment; the countermining the brief foregrounds is narration plus one trigger rather than playable content.
strengths: Defeat is correctly gated on the Town Center falling and on the loss of the garrison commander (Salm), the two outcomes the defenders actually faced.
Victory is a timed hold with a garrison-presence check rather than destruction of the besieger — exactly the goal a defender who only had to outlast the siege was set.

The sequence of narration follows the real siege: herald's summons to surrender, mining under the Carinthian bastion, mine detonation and breach, escalating assaults, Pashas' complaints of supply failure, October rains, retreat ordered 14 October.
123 STONE_WALL segments plus CASTLE, KEEP, GUARD_TOWERs and a gate give a credible medieval curtain-wall fortress for the player to defend.
ROMAN_RUINS is an apt nod to Vindobona underlying Vienna.
Landsknecht infantry rendered as PIKEMAN and CHAMPION is a reasonable engine abstraction of pike-and-halberd blocks.
justification: The event's shape is well reproduced in triggers and text — the herald's summons, the mine under the Carinthian bastion, three escalating assaults, the autumn rains and the 14 October withdrawal — and the win/lose conditions encode precisely the historical problem: hold the city until the besieger gives up, lose if the Town Center or Salm falls. The forces, however, are substantially off in avoidable ways: the arquebusiers are CROSSBOWMEN and the Ottoman assault troops are camel riders, light cavalry and cavalry archers with no janissary equivalent, while the engine offers HAND_CANNONEER and ELITE_JANISSARY; the bombard cannon and onagers also contradict the mine-driven siege the narration describes. Worst of all, both civilizations are left RANDOM, so nothing guarantees the Habsburg garrison or the Ottoman camp will look Central European or Turkish at all, and the map is smothered in 3,541 oaks where the Vienna plain and Ottoman trench lines should be.

  - DESTROY_OBJECT on RICHARD_THE_LIONHEART (player 1) [path "Defeat Hero"]
issues_found: Marco Polo is represented by the RICHARD_THE_LIONHEART hero object — a named twelfth-century English crusader king standing in for a thirteenth-century Venetian merchant. The engine offers no Polo hero, but a renamed generic villager, trade cart or camel would have been the correct substitution; using a different real historical figure is avoidable error.
Niccolo and Maffeo Polo have no representation on the map at all despite Niccolo being given dialogue lines; Player 1 has exactly one VILLAGER_MALE and no second hero or named companion.
Kublai Khan is entirely absent — there is no Khan unit, no Genghis/Khan hero, and no palace at the destination area (100,50)-(110,70); Shangdu is an empty patch of map.

The 'trade caravan' contains no trade carts and no pack animals whatsoever, though the brief states 'the caravan's pack animals must survive' and the engine ships TRADE_CART and CAMEL objects. The escort is instead 5 KNIGHTS, 5 CROSSBOWMEN and a CAVALIER — a Western European field detachment, not a merchant party.

Player 3 fields a BERSERK (Viking infantry) as the 'bandit chief' at a Central Asian oasis, and Players 3/4 use MILITIA and PIKEMEN — European foot troops for what should be Persian/Turkic/Karaunas raiders (Mamluk, camel, or cavalry-archer types were available).
Both active players are set to RANDOM civilization, so architecture and unit skins for the Mongol side are not guaranteed to be Mongol or Central Asian at all.

The scenario makes the Mongols the principal enemy — 'Ambush! The Khan's riders were waiting for us in the dunes!' — inverting the history: the Polos travelled under Kublai Khan's protection carrying his golden paiza, and Mongol patrols were their guarantors, not their attackers.

The journey's actual documented waypoints (Acre, Ayas, Hormuz, the Pamirs, the Gobi crossing, the three-and-a-half-year duration) are reduced to five anonymous 'D1–D5' area triggers with generic 'Halfway across the Silk Road' text.
strengths: The Mongol side (Player 2) is composed correctly for its type: 8 CAVALRY_ARCHER and 4 LIGHT_CAVALRY, with YURT_A–D and a palisade/gate outpost, which is a defensible rendering of a steppe encampment on the route.
Desert setting is at least gestured at with TREE_PALM_FOREST, ROCK_FORMATION and CLIFF objects, plus TENT_A/B and PAVILION_A for the caravan's own camp.
The victory condition — bring the protagonist hero object to a fixed eastern area representing Shangdu — is the correct historical goal, an arrival rather than an annihilation.
The defeat condition is the death of the protagonist, which is the loss the Polos actually risked on the road.

The escort/pursuit structure (timed Pursuit Waves, an oasis side-quest whose reward is CHANGE_OWNERSHIP of caravan guards) is a reasonable mechanical translation of a long overland journey under threat.
justification: The single most important object in the scenario is wrong: Marco Polo is played by RICHARD_THE_LIONHEART, a crusader king from a century earlier, when a renamed villager or trade cart was available; Niccolo speaks in dialogue but exists nowhere on the map, and Kublai Khan and his palace at Shangdu are absent from the victory area entirely. The 'trade caravan' has no trade carts or pack animals despite the brief hinging on them, and is instead 5 Knights and 5 Crossbowmen, while the bandit chief is a Viking BERSERK; both civilizations are left RANDOM, so even the Mongol yurts have no guaranteed architectural identity. The narration also inverts the history by making the Khan's own riders ambush the party the Khan had summoned and protected with a paiza. The encoded objective is the redeeming element — reach a specific eastern place, lose if the protagonist dies — which is genuinely the goal the history posed, even though the object being escorted is the wrong man.

The alternate timer victory (600s of holding) correctly encodes the defensive nature of Martel's task, and defeat on the commander's fall reflects the fragility of the Frankish cause.
Narration dates the action correctly to October 732 and names Charles Martel, Abd al-Rahman, Tours and Aquitania without inventing spurious episodes.
justification: The scenario's terrain, force composition and event arc are genuinely faithful — foot-heavy Franks in dense oak woods, all-cavalry Umayyads, a rallied Aquitanian force striking the camp, and victory turning on Abd al-Rahman's death exactly as the sources record. But every one of the three commanders is represented by the wrong named hero (William the Conqueror for Martel, Saladin for Abd al-Rahman, El Cid for Odo), which was entirely avoidable via renamed generics, and both players are left at RANDOM civilization so the architecture is unassigned. The invented Frankish TOWN_CENTER as a loss condition and the Umayyad CASTLE with 60 wall segments further contradict a battle fought on open high ground by a raiding army.

issues_found: The enemy commander is the SALADIN hero — a Kurdish sultan of Egypt/Syria active c. 1169-1193 in the Levant, with no connection to Iberia. The opponents of El Cid's exile years were al-Mundhir of Lerida/Denia, the Count of Barcelona Berenguer Ramon II, the Almoravids under Yusuf ibn Tashfin, and the Valencian qadi Ibn Jahhaf. Since the engine offers no Iberian-Muslim hero, a renamed generic Camel Rider or Cavalier would have been the correct stand-in; placing a different named historical hero is avoidable error.

Both players are set to civilization RANDOM, so architecture, unit sets and language are unassigned — Spanish for El Cid's retinue and Saracens (or Berbers) for the taifa/Almoravid side were both available.
37 CAMEL_RIDERs dominate the enemy army; Andalusi and Almoravid forces in eleventh-century Spain fought as light horse (jinetes) and Berber lancers, not massed camelry.
18 TREE_PALM_FOREST tiles give a Saharan/Levantine look rather than the Ebro valley and Levantine huerta around Zaragoza and Valencia.

El Cid's captain Minaya Alvar Fanez appears only in dialogue; the only representation is an unnamed generic KNIGHT whose death triggers defeat — a named or at least distinguished unit was trivially available.

The narrative spine is invented generic questing: a 'deeper plot against Zaragoza's throne', an 'Ambush Leader', a 'Traitor' who reveals himself, a 'Rescued Ally', and a 'Villain Confrontation' with 'Villain Speech'. None of this corresponds to the documented campaigns of 1081-94 (Almenar, Morella, the defeat and capture of Berenguer Ramon II at Tevar, the twenty-month blockade of Valencia).

The 1093-94 siege of Valencia is compressed into a single fortress storm with a duel against the enemy leader; in fact the city fell to a long starvation blockade and negotiated surrender, and the Almoravid relief army withdrew without battle.
Primary victory is the assassination of SALADIN, so the encoded goal rewards killing a man who was never in Spain rather than taking the city.
strengths: The EL_CID hero unit is correctly used for Rodrigo Diaz, and the engine does ship it.
Opening narration is chronologically correct: banishment from Castile by Alfonso VI in 1081, and service offered by 'Emir al-Mutamin' of Zaragoza, who did indeed hire El Cid.
Defeat on the death of El Cid matches the brief and the campaign's real dependence on his person.
An alternative victory on destroying the enemy CASTLE does encode the taking of Valencia, the correct historical endpoint.
Player 1's small mixed retinue (6 Men-at-Arms, 5 Pikemen, Knights/Cavalier, archers) reasonably represents a modest mercenary mesnada that grows by CHANGE_OWNERSHIP as allies join.
justification: The scenario gets the frame right in text — 1081, Alfonso VI's banishment, al-Mutamin's hire, Valencia as the prize — but the placed content contradicts it: the antagonist is the SALADIN hero, a twelfth-century Levantine sultan, backed by 37 camel riders among palm forests, with both civilizations left RANDOM. Primary victory is killing Saladin rather than taking Valencia (only an alternative condition), and the middle of the campaign is invented generic plotting (a 'Traitor', an 'Ambush Leader', a 'Villain Speech') in place of Almenar, Tevar, or the twenty-month blockade. An attentive player would leave believing El Cid's exile was spent fighting Saladin.

issues_found: Both players are set to RANDOM civilization, so the architecture set and unit bonuses are unpredictable — Britons/Franks (or Byzantines for Norman knights) were available and would have fixed Anglo-Saxon and Norman visual identity.

Harold Godwinson is represented by the generic KING unit, a non-combat, near-defenceless piece; the man who reportedly fought on foot in the shield wall until struck down is thus a passive object rather than a fighting champion-class stand-in.

Player 2 holds 44 STONE_WALL segments, a GATE and 4 GUARD_TOWERs. Harold's army fought on an unfortified ridge with no masonry whatsoever; the shield wall as stone curtain plus towers turns Senlac Hill into a castle-town siege.

4,174 oak trees smother a 120x120 map; the ridge above the Hastings marsh was open downland with the Andredsweald behind, not near-continuous forest, and heavy woods make the cavalry envelopment the brief promises impossible to stage.
Both sides have TOWN_CENTER, MILL, HOUSE, MONASTERY, BARRACKS, STABLE, ARCHERY_RANGE etc. — a settled economy neither invasion army nor the hastily assembled Saxon host possessed on the field.

16 SKIRMISHERs on the Saxon side overstates Anglo-Saxon missile troops, whose near-absence at Hastings was a decisive weakness; the Normans' archer arm (10 ARCHER vs 21 KNIGHT) is correspondingly underweighted.

Secondary victory VC2 awards the Norman player the battle simply for having a unit alive after 600 seconds — the nightfall deadline historically favoured Harold, whose army only had to hold until dark, so this inverts the clock.
Defeat on loss of the player's TOWN_CENTER is a generic AoE2 condition with no counterpart at Hastings; the Normans had no base to lose beyond the Pevensey/Hastings camp, which was never threatened.

The signature feigned retreats are only narrated in text; no trigger (PATROL/TASK_OBJECT) models a Norman withdrawal drawing the fyrd off the ridge, so the player never performs the tactic the brief centres on.
strengths: WILLIAM_THE_CONQUEROR is the correct engine hero for the Norman commander, and he is on the player's side as the brief states.

Force composition captures Norman combined arms (knights, man-at-arms, archers) against an infantry-only Saxon host of champions (housecarls) and spearmen (fyrd) with no cavalry at all — historically correct for Harold.
Primary victory is DESTROY_OBJECT on the enemy KING: the battle genuinely turned on Harold's death, and playing to win means doing what William's men did.
Defeat on William's death reflects the real fragility of the Norman position, when the rumour of his fall nearly routed his army until he bared his head.
Narration dates the action correctly (14 October 1066), names Senlac Hill, the marshy ground below the ridge, housecarls and fyrd levies, and the dusk deadline for a final assault.
Trigger [D9] fires 'The wall... it thins!' on OBJECTS_IN_AREA attrition, tying the collapse of the shield wall to actual losses rather than a bare timer.
justification: The scenario gets the parties, their asymmetric composition, and the decisive event right: a cavalry-and-archer Norman force under the correct William hero against an all-infantry Saxon host, with victory gated on killing Harold and defeat on William's death. It is undermined by an unassigned RANDOM civilization for both players, a Saxon position walled with 44 stone segments, a gate and four guard towers where no fortification existed, and 4,174 trees where there was open downland. The feigned retreats the brief makes central exist only as narration, and the alternate 600-second survival victory inverts a deadline that historically favoured the defenders.

issues_found: Player 1's hero is RICHARD_THE_LIONHEART standing in for Constantine XI Palaiologos, and Player 2's is SALADIN standing in for Mehmed II — two named Third Crusade figures transplanted into 1453. The engine ships no Constantine or Mehmed hero, so the correct choice was a renamed generic unit (e.g. a renamed Byzantine cataphract or an elite Janissary), not a different named hero.

Both active players are set to civilization RANDOM. The engine ships Byzantines and Turks; leaving the defenders and besiegers unassigned means the architecture set, unique units and bonuses are arbitrary — the walls may render as Japanese or Meso buildings.

Player 1's army is CROSSBOWMAN x10 and MAN_AT_ARMS x6 — a generic Feudal/Castle European garrison. No Byzantine-flavoured troops, no Genoese contingent under Giustiniani, and no gunpowder on either side.

Player 2 consists of a single hero unit at scenario start; the entire Ottoman army of some 60,000–80,000 exists only as timed CREATE_OBJECT waves, with no camp, no Ottoman siege park, and no bombard (the engine's BOMBARD_CANNON was available and is the single most iconic element of this siege — Orban's guns).
TREE_PALM_FOREST x20 for the Bosphorus shore; palms are wrong for Thrace.

The brief promises sea walls along the Golden Horn and a Hagia Sophia district, but nothing in the placed roster represents water, harbour, chain, ships, or a monumental church — the MONASTERY x1 is a generic production building, and the defeat condition keys on the CASTLE and TOWN_CENTER instead.

Assault waves come 'from the north', 'from the east', and 'from the south' — the Theodosian land walls face west; the historic breach was at the Mesoteichion/St Romanus gate on the western landward front.

The scenario's outcome inverts history: victory is holding until 'dawn' and Mehmed II saying 'their attack falters'. Constantinople fell on 29 May 1453 and Constantine XI died in the breach; a playthrough teaches the opposite.
GOLD_MINE x11, STONE_MINE x4, FORAGE_BUSH x8 and SHEEP x4 inside a besieged city are standard-random-map economy furniture, not a blockaded metropolis under famine.
strengths: STONE_WALL x120 with GATE_NORTH_TO_SOUTH x4 and GUARD_TOWER x8, plus a 'Close Gates' trigger, gives a genuine fortified perimeter appropriate to the Theodosian Walls.
The in-game text correctly names Constantine XI, Sultan Mehmed II, April 1453, and the Theodosian Walls.
The primary victory condition is a survival timer (600s) rather than annihilation of the besieger, which is the right shape of goal for a defensive siege.
Defeat keyed to the loss of a single fixed structure (the Castle / Town Center) correctly encodes that the defenders lose by losing the city, not by losing troops.
Escalating wave sizes (15 → 24 → 31 → 43 creates) with a 'siege engines approach' wave reflects the historical pattern of probing assaults building to a general storm.
justification: The text layer names the right people and date, but the placed content contradicts it at every point: Constantine XI is played by Richard the Lionheart and Mehmed II by Saladin, both avoidable errors since a renamed generic unit was the correct solution; both civilizations are left RANDOM despite Byzantines and Turks shipping with the game; the defenders field generic crossbowmen and men-at-arms while the Ottomans field no bombard cannon at all — omitting the one weapon that defined this siege. The setting is further undone by palm forest and by the complete absence of the Golden Horn sea walls and Hagia Sophia the brief promises. The survival-timer victory with defeat on loss of the central structure is the historically right kind of objective and earns credit, but the narration has Mehmed's assault falter and the city hold, inverting the actual outcome of 29 May 1453.

The English garrison of Troyes is built from CROSSBOWMAN, when the engine ships both Archer and the Briton Longbowman — the signature English missile arm — making the choice an avoidable mis-characterisation.

The escort column consists of 5 knights and 5 crossbowmen; the historical march to Reims was an army of roughly ten to twelve thousand, and no French captains of the march (Dunois, Alençon, La Hire, La Trémoille) appear even as renamed generics.
The 'ambush at the river crossing' near Chalons is invented: Chalons opened its gates to Charles without a fight, as did Troyes after negotiation.
The 'raider chief' side quest (Player 3 Champion + Militia, Player 4 pikemen villagers) is wholly fictional and has no counterpart in the June-July 1429 march.

2,880 oak trees blanket a map representing the open chalk plains and vineyards of Champagne.

The route is correct in sequence: departure after Orleans, midpoint at the Chalons river crossing, the walled garrison of Troyes, then Reims.
A MONASTERY placed as the goal is a reasonable engine proxy for Reims Cathedral, and the GAIA ROMAN_RUINS is apt for Roman-founded Durocortorum/Reims.
Death of the KING is a defeat condition — correctly encoding that without Charles there is no coronation.
Narration dates the march to June 1429 and names Orleans, Troyes, Chalons, Reims and the resulting title Charles VII accurately.
justification: The right principals are present — the engine's actual Joan of Arc hero escorting a KING as the Dauphin against a walled English garrison — and the geographic spine (Orleans, Troyes, Chalons, Reims) is faithfully ordered, with the King's death correctly a defeat. But both civilizations are left RANDOM, so the architecture of Champagne and of the English is undetermined when Frankish/Briton were available, the English garrison is armed with crossbowmen rather than the engine's longbowmen, and the map is smothered in nearly 3,000 oaks over open chalk plains. Events add an invented river ambush and a fictional 'raider chief' quest while omitting the historically decisive capitulation of Troyes, and victory is keyed to Joan entering Reims rather than to the Dauphin the coronation actually required.

issues_found: Marco Polo is represented by the EL_CID hero unit — a Castilian warlord who died in 1099, nearly two centuries before the journey; a renamed generic unit (or the Mongol/Persian civilian-style hero) would have avoided placing a different named historical figure on the map.
Niccolo Polo is represented by FREDERICK_BARBAROSSA, the 12th-century Holy Roman Emperor — again a wrong named figure where a renamed generic unit was available.
Kublai Khan, the destination and the second principal of the story, is never placed; Shangdu is only a Gaia TOWN_CENTER plus two yurts and flags, with no Khan figure or court at all.

Both active players are set to RANDOM civilization, so the Venetian party and the Central Asian bandits may render in any architecture set — Teutonic, Japanese, Mesoamerican — undoing the yurt/tent dressing.

The Polo escort is built as a feudal European war band (2 KNIGHT, 2 CROSSBOWMAN, 2 SPEARMAN); the historical party was a tiny merchant family group travelling with guides, not a mounted lance detachment.
Trade goods and pack animals are modelled as SHEEP when the engine ships TRADE_CART (and camels), which would represent a Silk Road caravan far more legibly — an avoidable choice.

The two bandit ambushes are generic invented set-pieces; the specific hazards the Polos recorded (the Karaunas raiders of Persia, the Gobi crossing, Niccolo's brother Maffeo's presence in the party) are absent, and Maffeo Polo is simply omitted.
strengths: Narration is factually sound: 1271 departure from Venice, Marco aged seventeen, the route via Persia and the Pamirs, four years of travel, seventeen years at the Khan's court.
The Pamir passage is called 'the Roof of the World', matching Polo's own account, and is implemented with CLIFF and ROCK_FORMATION terrain plus a resource grant at the crossing trigger.
Map dressing for the steppe/desert corridor is apt: YURT_A-D bandit camps, TENT/PAVILION for the caravan bivouac, TREE_PALM_FOREST, bonfires and torches.

The victory condition (bring Marco to the Shangdu area) and the two defeat conditions (Marco killed; all pack animals lost) encode exactly the historical stakes of the journey rather than a default 'kill the enemy' goal.
Bandits are cavalry archers, light cavalry and scouts — a defensible abstraction of Central Asian mounted raiders.
justification: The scenario's text and geography are genuinely well researched — 1271, a seventeen-year-old Marco, Persia and the Pamir 'Roof of the World', four years to Shangdu, seventeen years at court — and its trigger-encoded goal is precisely the historical one: escort a specific individual to a specific place, with defeat on his death or the loss of the caravan's animals. But the two principals are literally the wrong men: EL_CID stands in for Marco Polo and FREDERICK_BARBAROSSA for Niccolo, both avoidable since a renamed generic unit was available, while Kublai Khan is absent from his own palace. Leaving both players on RANDOM civilization further undercuts the yurt-and-tent dressing, and modelling a Silk Road caravan with sheep rather than the engine's trade carts is a missed opportunity rather than a limitation of the medium.

title: The Battle of Hastings

The feigned-retreat lure triggers and the fyrd's fatal downhill pursuit capture the battle's genuine turning point. The setting is where it falls down: both civilizations are left RANDOM, inviting wholly wrong architecture for eleventh-century Sussex, the ridge is buried under 4,480 trees, and Harold's position is garnished with a monastery and two guard towers that never existed there. Minor equipment errors (six crossbowmen in a 1066 Norman line) are avoidable given plain archers were on hand.

Abd al-Rahman al-Ghafiqi is represented by SALADIN, a named 12th-century Ayyubid sultan; the victory condition literally reads 'DESTROY_OBJECT on SALADIN'.
Duke Odo of Aquitaine is represented by EL_CID, an 11th-century Castilian figure — and one associated with the opposing (Iberian/Muslim-adjacent) side, compounding the confusion.

Both active players are set to civilization RANDOM, so Frankish and Umayyad architecture, unit availability, and bonuses are left to chance rather than assigned (Franks and Saracens/Berbers were all available).

Player 3 (the Aquitanians, nominally Frankish allies) is a purely cavalry force (6 Knights, 4 Scout Cavalry) with a Stable, while the Umayyad player fields Knights rather than any Frankish-side counterpart — the visual distinction between the sides is muddled.

Player 1's roster includes an ARCHERY_RANGE, CROSSBOWMAN x2 and a MONASTERY — crossbows are several centuries premature for an 8th-century Frankish host, and there is no reason to place them when spearmen/champions already carry the shield-wall role.
5,306 oak trees on a 120x120 map is a blunt-instrument representation of 'wooded high ground'; no elevation or terrain differentiation is evident from the placed content.
Force scale is tiny (roughly 17 Frankish and 16 Umayyad combatants) for an engagement of this reputation.
strengths: The Frankish player is built around infantry — Pikemen, Spearmen, Champions — correctly modelling the dismounted shield wall that held the ridge, against an all-mounted opponent (Knights, Camel Riders, Cavalry Archers).
The victory condition turns on killing the Umayyad commander, which is exactly the turning point the sources record: Abd al-Rahman's death broke the host.
Defeat conditions (the Frankish commander falls, or the camp is overrun) are the two losses that side actually faced, not a generic annihilation check.

The trigger sequence reproduces the shape of the battle: successive cavalry charges (Wave1, Wave2) breaking on a static line, then a flanking strike on the enemy baggage camp that triggers panic over the plunder.
The Odo rally is gated on BRING_OBJECT_TO_AREA with a messenger Villager, a concrete and period-appropriate mechanic rather than a timer.
Narration correctly dates the battle to October 732, places it on the Tours–Poitiers road, and ends with the Umayyad withdrawal south rather than inventing a Frankish counter-invasion.
justification: The scenario's structure is genuinely strong: infantry-versus-cavalry asymmetry, wave-based charges against a held line, a camp raid that panics the invaders over their plunder, and a victory keyed to the enemy commander's death — precisely the historical turning point, with defeat keyed to Martel's fall or the camp's loss. That accuracy is badly undercut by the cast: Charles Martel is WILLIAM_THE_CONQUEROR (1066), Abd al-Rahman is SALADIN (1180s), and Duke Odo is EL_CID (1090s), three avoidable anachronisms when renamed generic units would have served. Both active players are also left at RANDOM civilization, so the architecture and unit sets that would establish Francia and the Umayyad caliphate are unassigned. A player would absorb a broadly true account of 732 while staring at the wrong three famous men.

The opposing leader is the SALADIN hero, a twelfth-century Ayyubid sultan doing double duty for a Catalan count and a Valencian emir, when a renamed generic King or Camel Rider was available; both civilizations are left RANDOM, so the Castilian and Andalusi architecture is unspecified. The encoded victory condition is the death of that anachronistic hero rather than the capture of the city, turning a nine-month siege into a decapitation raid, and Valencia itself is a single Castle behind eight wall segments.

The narrative arc — Borte's abduction by Merkits, the Jamukha alliance and betrayal, the Naiman war, the 1206 kurultai on the Onon proclaiming Genghis Khan — matches the sources in shape and dates.

Victory keyed to slaying Tayang Khan of the Naiman is the specific turning point of 1204, not a generic wipe-out of all enemy objects.

Invented flavour (a forest ambush by 'English Scouts') and the mislabelling of the Burgundian towns as purely English add noise, though the narration is otherwise correctly dated and sequenced.

The 'Autumn Rains' message correctly identifies weather, supply failure and the short campaign season as the reasons the Ottoman host withdrew.
268 stone wall segments, a gate, keep, guard towers and castle give a genuine fortified-city defence rather than an open-field fight; ROMAN_RUINS is a nice nod to Vindobona beneath Vienna.
Pikemen as the Landsknecht core of the garrison is a fair engine abstraction.
justification: The scenario's narrative scaffolding is decent — countermining, three assaults on the Carinthian Gate, and the autumn rains that ended the siege are all there — but the placed content contradicts the text at almost every point that matters. The Sultan is Saladin and Salm is Frederick Barbarossa, two named heroes from three-and-a-half centuries earlier, when renamed generic units were available; both civilizations are RANDOM, so nothing about architecture or unit availability is period-anchored, and the arquebusiers the brief foregrounds appear as crossbowmen and skirmishers despite the engine shipping hand cannoneers. Most damagingly, victory is DESTROY_OBJECT on 'Saladin': a siege the defenders needed only to outlast is won by hunting down and killing the besieging sultan, who in fact survived and withdrew intact, and defeat is keyed to the death of a commander whose historical wounding did not lose the city.

issues_found: Marco Polo is represented by a KNIGHT and Niccolo/Maffeo by MAN_AT_ARMS — heavily armoured European military types for Venetian merchants; a Trade Cart, Villager, or even Monk-escorted civilian would have been a less misleading generic given the engine's catalogue (renaming is done correctly, however)

Shangdu is built as a GAIA CASTLE + TOWN_CENTER — a European donjon-and-town-centre silhouette for Kublai Khan's summer palace. A Mongol- or Chinese-owned set of buildings (Wonder, or Chinese/Mongol-architecture Town Center and walls) was available and would not have looked Frankish
Kublai Khan is a GAIA KING (renamed). Acceptable as a stand-in, but he is unowned and inert, so the Khan's court is scenery rather than a party to the event

Mongols are cast as the bandit raiders that ambush the caravan, which inverts the Pax Mongolica the Polos actually travelled under — Mongol authority is what made the route passable; the raiders on that stretch were local brigands, not the Khan's own people
Only 12 combat-capable units exist on a 120x120 map; the 'harsh terrain' threat named in the brief is represented purely by cliff decoration with no attrition or hazard mechanic
strengths: Player 1 is explicitly ITALIANS, the correct civilization for Venetian merchants, and Player 2 MONGOLS for the steppe
All three Polos are present and individually named via CHANGE_OBJECT_NAME, including Maffeo, who is usually dropped
Dating is correct throughout: departure 1271, 'more than three years of travel', audience with Kublai in 1275

Route geography is specific and in the right order — oasis, Taklamakan desert, Pamir high passes, plains of Cathay, Shangdu — reinforced by CLIFF and TREE_PALM_FOREST placement and staged BRING_OBJECT_TO_AREA narration
Victory is BRING_OBJECT_TO_AREA on Marco reaching the Shangdu area, not the destruction of an enemy — exactly the historical goal
Defeat conditions encode the three losses the expedition actually risked: Marco's death, the loss of the trade goods, and the death of both elder guides
Mongol camp is dressed with YURT_A–D and a Barracks rather than European housing
justification: The scenario gets the hard parts right: correct civilizations (Italians for Venice, Mongols for the steppe), all three named Polos as renamed generics rather than borrowed heroes, accurate 1271–1275 dating, and a waypointed route through Taklamakan, Pamir and Cathay to Shangdu. The objective graph is exemplary — victory turns on delivering Marco to the specific place, and defeat on losing Marco, the goods, or his guides, which is precisely what the expedition risked. Points come off for avoidable object choices: a KNIGHT and two MAN_AT_ARMS for merchants, SHEEP standing in for a pack train when Trade Carts exist, and a European GAIA CASTLE serving as Kublai's summer palace. Casting Mongols as the ambushing bandits also muddles the Pax Mongolica that in fact protected the route.

title: The Battle of Hastings
objective_facts:
EXTRACTED VICTORY AND DEFEAT CONDITIONS
(taken directly from the trigger graph; score `objective` from

Victory:
  - DESTROY_OBJECT on KING (player 2) [path "VC - Harold Slain"]
Defeat:

issues_found: Both players are set to RANDOM civilization, so the Normans may appear with Japanese, Aztec, or Turkish architecture and receive a wholly inappropriate tech/unit profile; Franks (or Britons for Harold) were available and should have been assigned explicitly.
4,800 oak trees on a 120x120 map turns Senlac Hill into dense woodland; the battle was fought on an open ridge above marshy ground, with the Andredsweald only behind the Saxon line.
Standard random-map economic furniture (10 gold mines, 8 stone mines, 16 forage bushes, sheep, deer) is present in a one-day field battle where no economy existed.
Player 2's two Guard Towers and a Monastery imply fortification and a garrison position; Harold's army arrived and formed an unfortified shield wall on the ridge with no stone works.
Both sides are given Town Centers, an artefact of standard map generation rather than anything at Hastings.
Norman force ratio is inverted: 20 Knights but only 10 Man-at-Arms and 14 Archers. William's largest contingent was infantry, with cavalry perhaps a third of the host.
Player 2 is given 4 Archers; Anglo-Saxon missile troops at Hastings were negligible and the sources emphasise their near-total absence.

The 'Feigned Retreat Draws the Housecarls' trigger only prints text on OBJECTS_IN_AREA; nothing actually pulls Saxon units off the line, so the battle's decisive tactic is asserted rather than modelled.
No representation of Harold's brothers Gyrth and Leofwine, or of the Malfosse pursuit that ended the day.
strengths: WILLIAM_THE_CONQUEROR is the correct named hero for the Norman commander, not a substituted figure from another century.
Harold is a generic KING renamed 'Harold Godwinson' by trigger, the right approach where the engine ships no hero for him.
Saxon roster of 20 Champions (axe-armed housecarls) plus 20 Spearmen and zero cavalry correctly reflects a dismounted shield wall with no mounted arm.
Victory is gated on destroying Harold specifically, which is exactly how the battle was decided.
Defeat on William's death matches the real crisis in the Norman centre when William was rumoured slain.
A 1500-second nightfall timer defeat encodes the genuine constraint that Harold needed only to hold the ridge until dark.
Narration dates the action correctly to 14 October 1066 and names Senlac Hill, the road to London, and the feigned-flight tactic.
justification: The combatant modelling is strong: the correct named Norman hero, a properly renamed King standing in for Harold, and an all-infantry Saxon roster of Champions and Spearmen, marred only by an inverted Norman knight-to-infantry ratio and four Saxon archers. The victory and defeat conditions are the historical ones almost exactly — kill Harold, lose if William falls or if the sun sets on an intact shield wall. Setting is the weak point: both civilizations are left RANDOM, so architecture and unit availability are unpredictable, and the map is buried under 4,800 trees with gold mines, stone mines, Guard Towers and a Monastery that belong to a random-map skirmish rather than an open ridge in Sussex. Events follow the correct shape and the feigned retreat is narrated, though that turning point is only a text message and never mechanically drags housecarls out of the line.

All three distinct antagonists — al-Mutamin's Zaragoza (ally), Berenguer Ramon II of Barcelona (enemy), and Ibn Jahhaf's Valencia (target) — are collapsed into a single Player 2 roster, so the player's Muslim patron is indistinguishable from his Muslim and Christian enemies

strengths: Chronology in the narration is correct and specific: banishment by Alfonso VI in 1081, service to al-Mutamin ibn Hud of Zaragoza, Almenar, the 1090 battle of Tébar with the capture of Berenguer Ramon II, the 1092 siege and 1094 fall of Valencia under qadi Ibn Jahhaf

Muslim contingents are differentiated with CAMEL_RIDER and CAVALRY_ARCHER against the Christian KNIGHT/CROSSBOWMAN/SPEARMAN retinue, a reasonable engine approximation of Andalusi versus Castilian troops

Trigger sequence follows the historical order — march to Zaragoza, coalition battle, march south, siege, gate breached, city taken — with a reward of extra troops after the Barcelona victory reflecting the growth of his retinue

But the placed content contradicts the text at the level that matters: El Cid is an anonymous CHAMPION when the editor ships an actual El Cid hero, the player is FRANKS instead of SPANISH, Player 2's civilisation is RANDOM so no taifa architecture is guaranteed, and Zaragoza, Barcelona and Valencia are all one undifferentiated player whose 'leaders' are unnamed KING objects. The result reads accurately and plays generically.

TREE_PALM_FOREST on the map is wrong flora for the Thracian/Marmara littoral and reads as a desert-set filler

Named leaders are handled properly: generic KING units stand in for Constantine XI and Mehmed II rather than importing an unrelated named hero, and a CHAMPION serves as Giovanni Giustiniani
Defeat is keyed to the destruction of a MONASTERY standing for Hagia Sophia — a place-specific loss condition rather than a generic unit wipe
Victory is survival on a timer, the correct encoding for a siege the defenders had only to outlast

justification: The trigger chain reproduces the siege's actual shape — cannon breach at St. Romanus, the Golden Horn probe, Giustiniani's loss, the 29 May general assault — and encodes exactly the right goal: hold out on a timer, lose if Hagia Sophia (a Monastery) falls. It is undercut by the build itself: both civilizations are left RANDOM, so no Byzantine or Turkish architecture or unique units appear, and the promised Janissaries are placed as ten generic MAN_AT_ARMS when the engine offers the Janissary outright. The Golden Horn sea walls have no water or ships behind them, palm forest is wrong for Thrace, and an even 30-vs-31 force ratio erases the overwhelming numerical asymmetry that defined 1453.

issues_found: Both active players are set to RANDOM civilization. The engine ships a Mongols civ (and Tatars/Huns as alternatives); leaving Temujin's own tribe as a random draw means his warband and any built architecture may be Frankish, Teutonic or Japanese, an entirely avoidable error.
SUBOTAI is placed in Temujin's starting warband dated 1186. Subutai was born c. 1175 and entered Temujin's service in the late 1190s; he did not ride with the Borjigin warband of 1186.

All four opponents — the Merkit, Jamukha's Jadaran, the 'Naiman-aligned outpost' and Tayang Khan's Naiman — are lumped into a single Player Two. The anda alliance and its rupture are handled only by CHANGE_OWNERSHIP, so the player never faces distinct tribal confederations as the history requires.

The Merkit/enemy camp is enclosed with PALISADE_WALL x8 and a GATE_NORTH_TO_SOUTH. Steppe nomad camps of the period were unwalled yurt encampments; the engine's yurts alone (already used) would have been correct.
Enemy chiefs (Merkit chief, Jamukha, Tayang Khan) are represented by KING units — dismounted sedentary monarchs for mounted steppe chieftains — when a renamed cavalry or Khan-type unit was available.

The war against Toghrul/Wang Khan of the Kereit (1203), the decisive campaign before the Naiman war, is entirely absent; the Kereit appear only as a passing text mention as allies, and the Tatar campaigns are omitted too.

The break with Jamukha is triggered by an invented event — raiding a 'Naiman-aligned outpost to prove your strength'. The historical rupture followed Dalan Balzhut and Jamukha's election as Gur-khan in 1201, not a scripted raid.

Victory is UNCONDITIONAL and fires on no condition, so the encoded goal is not the kurultai proclamation the objective text and history point to; nothing in the trigger graph makes winning depend on reaching the gathering ground or slaying Tayang Khan.
strengths: Defeat is correctly gated on the death of Temujin (GENGHIS_KHAN, player 1) — the loss that side genuinely faced, since the confederation depended wholly on his survival.
Steppe setting is dressed with the right props: YURT_A–D encampments for every faction, sheep and deer herds, rock formations and no stone-city architecture.
Force composition is appropriately horse-centric: light cavalry and scout cavalry for Temujin, 13 cavalry archers for the enemy, with no infantry or siege.

The narrative beats and dates are essentially correct: Borte's abduction by the Merkit, the Kereit assistance in her rescue, the anda oath with Jamukha, Jamukha's defection to Tayang Khan, the Naiman collapse in 1204 and the kurultai of 1206.
A small starting warband growing by ownership transfer after the alliance mirrors how Temujin's horde actually accreted through tribal submissions.
justification: The narrative spine is sound — Borte's rescue with Kereit help, the anda with Jamukha and its rupture, Tayang Khan's death in 1204, the kurultai of 1206 — and the roster is properly horse-archer and yurt-based, with the correct defeat condition on Temujin's own life. But both players are left on RANDOM civilization despite a Mongols civ being available, the enemy camp is palisaded like a European village, Subutai is placed in a 1186 warband a decade before he joined, and every opposing tribe is one undifferentiated Player Two whose chiefs are KING units. Most damagingly, the victory trigger is UNCONDITIONAL on no condition, so the encoded goal is neither the kurultai nor even the generic destruction of the Naiman — it is nothing at all.

title: The Road to Reims
objective_facts:

issues_found: Troyes and Chalons were held by Anglo-Burgundian garrisons loyal to Philip the Good as much as to Henry VI; assigning them wholly to a BRITONS player and having them shout 'Champagne remains loyal to King Henry' erases the Burgundian dimension that actually made the towns negotiable.

No named commander on either side except Joan: the French column has no Duke d'Alencon, La Hire or Dunois although the engine ships heroes for all three and all three rode with the Reims column, so their absence is avoidable.

The brief's 'can be fought or persuaded to surrender' mechanic is not implemented: the only garrison triggers are TIMER-driven PATROL sorties and DESTROY_OBJECT checks, so Troyes is 'fallen' and Chalons 'taken' by force, whereas historically Troyes capitulated after negotiation and a bluffed assault and Chalons opened its gates without a fight.

Force scale is very thin for the event: 12 French combat units (4 knights, 4 crossbowmen, 4 spearmen) stand in for an army of some ten thousand, and each 'garrison' is 2 castles with about 8 defenders.
7,574 oak trees dominate a 120x120 map representing the open chalk plains and vineyards of Champagne; the route Auxerre-Troyes-Chalons-Reims was notably open country, not near-continuous forest.
The 'English rider spurs for Troyes' warning is invented flavour with no source basis.
strengths: Correct principals and sides: FRANKS versus BRITONS with the engine's own JOAN_OF_ARC hero rather than a substitute or wrong-century stand-in.
The Dauphin is represented by the KING unit and renamed via a setup CHANGE_OBJECT_NAME trigger, exactly the right use of the engine's catalogue for a figure with no hero.
Victory is BRING_OBJECT_TO_AREA on the KING at the Reims cathedral area and defeat is DESTROY_OBJECT on the KING - precisely the historical stake: the coronation happens or the cause of France ends.
A GAIA MONASTERY stands in for Reims Cathedral, a sensible engine substitute for the coronation site.
Waypointed narration in the correct geographic and chronological order (Orleans aftermath, Troyes, Chalons, Reims) and the closing text dates the coronation correctly to 17 July 1429.
Bypassing rather than storming the garrisons is mechanically possible, since the win condition never requires their destruction.
justification: The scenario names the right parties and the right heroine, uses the KING unit renamed as the Dauphin, and encodes the historical stake exactly: bring Charles to the Reims cathedral area to win, lose him to lose. Its weaknesses are avoidable rather than engine-imposed: the Champagne towns are made purely English rather than Anglo-Burgundian, the promised surrender-by-persuasion path is absent so both garrisons must be destroyed or evaded, no French captains (d'Alencon, La Hire, Dunois all exist as heroes) ride with the column, and the map buries open Champagne under 7,500 oaks. Play would still leave an attentive player with a broadly true picture of the march and its correctly dated outcome.
